questions.question: For a system deployed with rolling upgrades, why does how a data encoding handles schema changes usually matter more than small differences in encoded size?

options.text: Old and new versions of code and data coexist, so each version must be able to read data written by the other
All binary formats produce roughly the same size, so encoded size no longer distinguishes one format from another
Smaller encodings are automatically easier to evolve, so optimizing for size also delivers compatibility
Encoded size matters only for network transfer, and a rolling upgrade never sends encoded data over the network

questions.explanation: Applications change continually, and during a rolling upgrade some nodes run new code while others still run old code, all touching the same stored data and messages. The system keeps working only if new code can read old data (backward compatibility) and old code can read new data (forward compatibility). Size still matters at scale, but formats do differ in size (the same record can take 81 bytes as JSON and 32 bytes in Avro), and a compact format with no evolution story can still break a deployment.

questions.question: Why do an application's features, and therefore the data it stores, typically need to change over time? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: New products are launched
User requirements become better understood
Business circumstances change
Relational databases require the schema to be redefined on every deployment

questions.explanation: Applications change because the products, the understanding of users' needs, and the business around them change. Those feature changes usually require new fields or new interpretations of stored data, so data encodings must support old and new code coexisting. Treating change as normal (evolvability) is the design goal, rather than assuming one permanent representation.

optionExplanations.a: A new product introduces capabilities and domain concepts that existing data structures did not capture. The encoding must evolve so old and new versions can coexist during rollout.
optionExplanations.b: Teams learn what users actually need after observing real behavior, so fields and interpretations change as understanding improves. Assuming the first schema is permanent would block that learning.
optionExplanations.c: Markets, regulations, partnerships, and operating models change what the business must record and exchange. Data representations therefore need planned evolution rather than one final design.
optionExplanations.d: Relational databases keep one schema in force and change it only through explicit migrations such as ALTER statements; deployments do not force a redefinition. Change is driven by product and business needs, not by the database mechanism.

questions.question: When a new application feature requires a change to the data the application stores, what kinds of data change does that typically involve? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A new field or record type needs to be captured
Existing data needs to be presented in a new way
Every existing record must be rewritten into the new format before the feature ships
The encoding library must be replaced with a different one

questions.explanation: Feature changes alter data in two common ways: the application starts capturing new fields or record types, or it needs to interpret and present existing data differently. Neither requires immediately rewriting all stored data or swapping the encoding library; instead, readers and writers temporarily disagree about the data's shape, which is why compatibility rules are needed.

optionExplanations.a: Capturing a new fact requires an additional field or record type that older writers never produced. Readers must define what absence means while versions overlap.
optionExplanations.b: A new view or interpretation may require existing data to be decoded, combined, or exposed differently. Evolution concerns how data is consumed as well as what is newly stored.
optionExplanations.c: Rewriting all existing data is expensive on large datasets and usually avoided; old records typically stay in their original encoding and are handled through compatibility rules such as defaults for missing fields.
optionExplanations.d: A good encoding format supports schema evolution, so adding fields or changing interpretation does not require switching libraries. The schema changes; the format and library usually stay the same.

questions.question: How do relational databases and schema-on-read (schemaless) document databases differ in how they cope with a change to the data format?

options.text: Relational: one schema at a time, changed by migrations; schema-on-read: old and new formats can coexist
Relational: several schema versions coexist until a migration runs; schema-on-read: one format is enforced on write
Both enforce one schema at a time; schema-on-read databases just run their migrations lazily in the background
Neither has any notion of format; both leave all interpretation of stored data entirely to the application

questions.explanation: A relational database assumes all its data conforms to one schema. That schema can be changed through schema migrations (ALTER statements), but exactly one schema is in force at any moment. A schema-on-read database does not enforce a schema, so it can hold a mixture of records written in older and newer formats at different times, and the reading code must cope with that mixture. The common misconception is that schemaless means no format at all; it means the structure is interpreted when read rather than enforced when written.

questions.question: What is a rolling upgrade (staged rollout) of a server-side application, and what does it make possible?

options.text: Deploying the new version to a few nodes at a time and checking it before continuing; it allows releases without downtime
Standing up a full parallel cluster on the new version and switching all traffic at once; it avoids running mixed versions
Upgrading every node simultaneously during a maintenance window; it guarantees that all nodes agree on one version
Upgrading the database schema on all nodes first and the code later; it removes the need for any data migration

questions.explanation: In a rolling upgrade, the new version is deployed to a few nodes at a time; operators check that it runs smoothly and gradually work through the whole fleet. Because the rest of the fleet keeps serving traffic, there is no service downtime, which encourages more frequent releases. The consequence is that old and new versions of the code run side by side for a while, which is why backward and forward compatibility of data matter.

questions.question: Why can't the operator of a client-side application (such as a mobile app) retire old versions on a schedule the way a server-side rolling upgrade does?

options.text: Users decide when, or whether, to install an update, so old client versions may keep running indefinitely
Client code cannot carry a version number, so the server has no way to tell old and new clients apart
Client devices cannot store data locally, so there is no data on them that could be migrated forward
Clients only ever talk to the newest server, so old client versions are rejected and disappear automatically

questions.explanation: Server operators control when server processes are replaced, but users may postpone or permanently skip a client update. Old clients must therefore keep working against newer services and newer data, because no deployment mechanism can force every device to upgrade. This makes long-lived compatibility a requirement rather than a temporary concern.

questions.question: In the context of data encoding, what do backward compatibility and forward compatibility mean?

options.text: Backward: newer code can read data written by older code. Forward: older code can read data written by newer code
Backward: older code can read data written by newer code. Forward: newer code can read data written by older code
Backward: data can be downgraded to an older schema. Forward: data can be upgraded to a newer schema in place
Backward: newer code can write data in the old format. Forward: older code can write data in the new format

questions.explanation: Both terms are about reading data across versions. Backward compatibility means newer code can read data that older code wrote; it looks back at old data. Forward compatibility means older code can read data that newer code wrote; it copes with data from the future. The two are often swapped, and neither is about converting stored data or about which version writes which format. During a rolling upgrade both are needed at once.

questions.question: Of backward and forward compatibility, which is usually easier to achieve, and why?

options.text: Backward: new code's authors know the old format; forward needs old code to ignore additions
Forward: old code can simply reject anything unfamiliar, while backward requires rewriting all of the old data
Neither: both are equally hard, because each code version must know the full format used by the other
Backward is harder, because old formats are rarely documented, while forward follows automatically from a schema

questions.explanation: Backward compatibility is normally not hard: whoever writes the newer code knows what data the older code wrote and can explicitly handle it, if necessary by keeping the old reading logic. Forward compatibility is trickier because the old code was written before the new format existed; it can only cope if it was designed to ignore additions it does not understand. Rejecting unfamiliar data is the opposite of forward compatibility.

questions.question: During a rolling upgrade, a node still running the old version of the code reads a record written by a node already running the new version. Which compatibility property does this read rely on?

options.text: Backward compatibility, because the data was written by newer code
Forward compatibility, because older code is reading newer data
Backward compatibility, because older code is doing the reading
Version isolation: nodes only read records written by their own version

questions.explanation: Older code reading data written by newer code is forward compatibility. A rolling upgrade means the cluster deliberately runs mixed versions, so nodes do not share one schema version. The reverse case, an upgraded node reading a record that an old node wrote, relies on backward compatibility; a rolling upgrade needs both, but this particular read needs forward.

questions.question: Which of these encodings provide a defined mechanism, such as numeric field tags or writer/reader schema resolution, for evolving a schema while old and new code coexist? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Protocol Buffers
Apache Thrift
Apache Avro
Java's built-in serialization (java.io.Serializable)

questions.explanation: Protocol Buffers and Thrift identify fields by numeric tags in a schema, with clear rules for adding and removing fields. Avro resolves the writer's schema against the reader's schema by field name, using defaults for missing fields. Language built-in serialization such as Java's tends to treat versioning as an afterthought, so it does not give dependable forward and backward compatibility.

optionExplanations.a: Protocol Buffers identifies each field by a tag number, so new fields get fresh tags, old readers skip unknown tags, and names can change freely. These rules give defined forward and backward compatibility.
optionExplanations.b: Thrift uses the same tag-number principle as Protocol Buffers, so its schemas evolve under the same rules: new fields optional with new tags, removed tags never reused.
optionExplanations.c: Avro has no tags but resolves the writer's schema against the reader's schema by field name, ignoring writer-only fields and filling reader-only fields from defaults. That resolution is an explicit evolution mechanism.
optionExplanations.d: Java serialization is tied to Java classes and was designed for quick, convenient encoding; versioning is largely an afterthought and it is notorious for poor performance and bloated output. It lacks a dependable cross-version evolution model.

questions.question: Programs usually work with data in two different representations. What are they, and why do they differ?

options.text: In-memory structures that use pointers for fast CPU access, and a self-contained byte sequence for files or the network
A compressed form for storage and an uncompressed form for computation, each chosen to save space or time
A row-oriented layout for transactions and a column-oriented layout for analytics, each suiting its query load
An encrypted form for transmission and a plaintext form for processing, each chosen for security or speed

questions.explanation: In memory, data lives in objects, structs, lists, hash tables, and trees, optimized for efficient CPU access and typically linked by pointers. To write data to a file or send it over the network, it must become a self-contained sequence of bytes, because a pointer means nothing to another process. Translating between the two is encoding and decoding; compression, column layout, and encryption are separate concerns.

questions.question: Which exceptions allow an encoded or on-disk representation to double as the representation operated on in memory? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A memory-mapped file whose bytes are accessed directly through virtual memory
A column store that performs operations directly on compressed column data
Any two processes that happen to share memory, regardless of data layout
Any record smaller than one virtual-memory page

questions.explanation: Programs usually decode a self-contained byte sequence into pointer-rich in-memory structures. Memory mapping and direct processing of compressed columns are exceptions because the stored bytes themselves become the structure being accessed, avoiding a conventional decode into a separate representation.

optionExplanations.a: A memory-mapped file exposes stored bytes through virtual memory so code can access the mapped layout directly. The on-disk and in-memory views can therefore be the same representation.
optionExplanations.b: Some column engines execute filters and aggregates directly over compressed column blocks. Avoiding full decompression means the encoded storage layout remains the structure being operated on.
optionExplanations.c: Sharing an address space does not make an arbitrary byte encoding identical to pointer-rich runtime objects. The processes still need an agreed layout and may need decoding.
optionExplanations.d: Fitting inside one virtual-memory page changes I/O granularity, not the relationship between encoded bytes and runtime structures. Small records normally still require parsing into usable values.

questions.question: What are the terms for translating an in-memory data structure into a byte sequence, and for translating it back?

options.text: Encoding (serialization, marshalling), and decoding (parsing, deserialization, unmarshalling)
Compression (deflating, zipping), and decompression (inflating, unzipping)
Encryption (enciphering, sealing), and decryption (deciphering, unsealing)
Hashing (digesting, fingerprinting), and verification (checking, validating)

questions.explanation: Turning an in-memory representation into a byte sequence is called encoding, also known as serialization or marshalling; the reverse is decoding, also called parsing, deserialization, or unmarshalling. Encoding only changes representation. It has nothing to do with encryption: it does not provide secrecy or integrity, and it need not reduce size the way compression does.

questions.question: Why might a text on data systems prefer the word 'encoding' over the more common 'serialization' for converting data into bytes?

options.text: 'Serialization' also names a transaction isolation concept (serializability) with a completely different meaning
'Serialization' describes only text formats, whereas 'encoding' also covers the compact binary formats
'Serialization' implies the data stays within one programming language, unlike cross-language formats
'Encoding' also implies that the data is encrypted, which makes it the more precise and complete term

questions.explanation: In the context of transactions, serializability (serializable isolation) means concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, which has nothing to do with converting data into bytes. To avoid overloading one word with two meanings, 'encoding' is used for the byte conversion, even though 'serialization' is probably the more common term. Encoding is unrelated to encryption, and serialization covers both text and binary, single-language and cross-language formats.

questions.question: Which of these are language-specific object-encoding facilities, whose output is tied to one programming language? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: java.io.Serializable in Java (and third-party libraries such as Kryo)
Marshal in Ruby
pickle in Python
JSON.stringify in JavaScript

questions.explanation: Java's Serializable (and Java libraries like Kryo), Ruby's Marshal, and Python's pickle encode language-specific object graphs. They are convenient within one ecosystem but tie stored or transmitted data to that language, and often have weak compatibility and security properties. JSON.stringify is a JavaScript API, but its output is standard JSON that any language can read.

optionExplanations.a: Java's Serializable and Kryo preserve Java-specific object graphs and classes with little application code. That convenience couples stored data to Java types and library behavior.
optionExplanations.b: Ruby's Marshal saves and restores Ruby object structures, including language-specific type information. Other languages cannot generally decode it without reproducing Ruby semantics.
optionExplanations.c: Python's pickle serializes Python objects and can invoke executable reconstruction behavior while loading. It is convenient but language-bound and unsafe for untrusted input.
optionExplanations.d: JSON.stringify emits standardized JSON rather than a JavaScript-only object encoding and does not preserve arbitrary prototypes or runtime object identity. Its API is JavaScript-specific, but the resulting format is language independent.

questions.question: What is the main attraction of a programming language's built-in object encoding (such as Java serialization or Python pickle), and what is its most basic drawback?

options.text: Objects are saved and restored with minimal code, but the encoding ties the data to that one language
It is the fastest encoding available, but its format has never been formally standardized
It handles schema evolution automatically, but its encoded output is more verbose than JSON
Any language can read its output, but decoding untrusted input with it is insecure

questions.explanation: Built-in encoders are convenient: in-memory objects can be saved and restored with almost no extra code. The basic problem is that the encoding is usually tied to one language, so reading it from another language is very difficult. Storing or transmitting data this way commits you to your current language for a long time and hinders integration with other organizations' systems. They are also often slow, weak on versioning, and a security risk.

questions.question: Why is decoding untrusted input with a language's built-in serialization (for example Java serialization or Python pickle) a security risk?

options.text: The decoder instantiates arbitrary classes, which an attacker can exploit to run code
The encoding is plaintext, so anyone watching the network can read the data in transit
The encoding embeds memory addresses, which leaks the layout of the process heap
The encoding cannot carry a checksum, so tampering with bytes goes undetected

questions.explanation: To restore data into the same object types, the decoder must be able to instantiate arbitrary classes named in the byte stream. If an attacker can get an application to decode a byte sequence of their choosing, they can make it instantiate classes it never intended to, which often leads to remote code execution. The danger comes from what the decoder does, not from the data being visible or unchecked on the wire.

questions.question: Besides language lock-in and security risks, what other weaknesses do language built-in serialization libraries typically have?

options.text: Versioning is an afterthought, and efficiency is poor; Java's built-in serialization is notoriously slow and bloated
They cannot encode nested objects, and they need a separate schema compiler before anything can be encoded
They are never thread-safe, and their encoded output cannot be sent over a network connection at all
They produce only human-readable text, and they always lose precision on floating-point numbers

questions.explanation: Because these libraries aim at quick and easy encoding, they often neglect the inconvenient problems of forward and backward compatibility, so changing a class can make old data unreadable. Efficiency, both CPU time and encoded size, is also often an afterthought; Java's built-in serialization is notorious for bad performance and bloated output. Together with lock-in and security, this makes them a poor choice for anything long-lived.

questions.question: When is it reasonable to use a programming language's built-in object encoding?

options.text: Only for very transient data, not for anything stored or shared
Whenever both endpoints happen to be written in the same language
For long-term storage, as long as network traffic uses another format
Whenever the data is too large or too complex to encode as JSON

questions.explanation: Because built-in encodings tie data to one language, neglect versioning, perform poorly, and can be exploited, it is generally a bad idea to use them for anything other than very transient purposes. Sharing a language today does not protect stored data from class changes or a later language change, and long-term storage is exactly where versioning matters most. The Akka actor framework, for instance, uses Java serialization by default and so loses the ability to do rolling upgrades unless that is replaced.

questions.question: Why did JSON become more popular than XML as a textual data format?

options.text: Browsers support it natively, as a subset of JavaScript, and it is simpler than XML
It distinguishes integers from floating-point numbers precisely, which XML cannot do
It comes with a mandatory schema language, which XML has never had
It supports binary strings natively, so no Base64 workaround is ever needed

questions.explanation: JSON's popularity comes mainly from built-in support in web browsers, because it is a subset of JavaScript, and from its simplicity relative to XML, which is often criticized as verbose and complicated. JSON does not distinguish integers from floats, has only an optional schema language, and lacks binary strings, so its success is not due to type precision.

questions.question: How well do XML, CSV, and JSON distinguish between kinds of numeric values?

options.text: XML/CSV can't tell a number from a digit string without a schema; JSON can't tell integers from floats
XML and CSV mark numbers natively; JSON stores every value, including numbers, as a quoted string
All three distinguish integers from floats, but none of them specifies the precision of a number
JSON distinguishes integers from floats; XML and CSV tell numbers from strings but not integer from float

questions.explanation: Without an external schema, XML and CSV cannot distinguish a number from a string that happens to consist of digits. JSON does distinguish strings from numbers, but it does not distinguish integers from floating-point numbers and does not specify a precision. As a result a large integer written by one program may be read inexactly by another, for example by JavaScript, which parses numbers as doubles.

questions.question: Why can a JavaScript client receiving JSON lose precision when it parses a very large integer, such as a 64-bit ID?

options.text: JavaScript parses it as an IEEE 754 double, exact only up to 2^53
JSON limits integers to the unsigned 32-bit range, truncating larger ones
JSON parsers store numbers as Base64 text, which rounds values beyond 2^64
HTTP converts every numeric value in a body into a signed 31-bit integer

questions.explanation: IEEE 754 double precision has 53 bits of integer precision, so integers greater than 2^53 (9,007,199,254,740,992) cannot all be represented exactly; a parser that uses doubles silently rounds them. Twitter's 64-bit tweet IDs exceed that, so its API returned each ID twice, as a JSON number and as a decimal string, letting JavaScript clients use the exact string.

questions.question: JSON and XML have no type for binary strings (raw byte sequences). What is the usual workaround, and roughly how much larger does it make the data?

options.text: Base64-encode the bytes as text, making them about 33% larger
Hex-encode the bytes as text, making them about 33% larger
Base64-encode the bytes as text, making them about 100% larger
Put the raw bytes in an XML CDATA section, with no size increase

questions.explanation: Binary data is usually encoded as text using Base64, and a schema or convention says the value should be interpreted as Base64. Base64 represents every 3 bytes as 4 characters, a ratio of 4/3, so the data grows by about 33%. Hex encoding uses 2 characters per byte, doubling the size. CDATA cannot hold arbitrary bytes, because XML text must consist of valid characters.

questions.question: What is the state of schema support for XML and JSON?

options.text: Both have optional, powerful but complex schema languages; XML's are widely used, JSON's often skipped
Both require a schema for parsing, so applications never need to hardcode how values are interpreted
Only XML has a schema language; JSON data can only ever be interpreted by informal convention
JSON Schema is used by nearly all JSON tools, while XML Schema is rarely used in practice

questions.explanation: Schema languages exist for both XML and JSON but are optional. They are quite powerful and therefore complicated to learn and implement. Use of XML Schema is fairly widespread, but many JSON-based tools don't bother with schemas. Since the correct interpretation of numbers and binary strings depends on schema information, applications without a schema must hardcode the encoding and decoding logic instead.

questions.question: Which of these are genuine weaknesses of CSV as a data format? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It has no schema, so the application must define what each row and column means
If an application change adds a row or column, the change must be handled manually
Its escaping rules for commas and newlines are specified, but not all parsers implement them correctly
It requires every value to be quoted, which makes files larger than the same data as JSON

questions.explanation: CSV has no schema, so the meaning of each row and column lives in application code, and any added row or column has to be handled manually by every reader. It is also a vague format: what happens if a value contains a comma or newline? Escaping rules have been formally specified (RFC 4180), but not all parsers implement them correctly. Quoting is optional, used only where needed.

optionExplanations.a: CSV carries no built-in types or constraints, so applications must agree separately on what each position means. A parser can split fields without understanding the record's meaning.
optionExplanations.b: Because CSV has no evolution metadata or field tags, adding a column or row shape requires application-specific handling. Old readers cannot infer how the positions changed.
optionExplanations.c: RFC 4180 defines quoting for commas and newlines, but implementations differ in how completely they follow it. The practical ambiguity comes from inconsistent parsers, not total absence of a specification.
optionExplanations.d: CSV quotes a value only when it contains a delimiter, quote, or newline; most values are written bare. CSV usually omits field names per row, so it is often smaller than equivalent JSON, not larger.

questions.question: Why are JSON, XML, and CSV likely to stay popular for sending data between different organizations, despite their flaws?

options.text: Getting organizations to agree on any format is the hard part, outweighing elegance or efficiency
Textual formats parse faster than binary ones, which matters most when data crosses organizational boundaries
Only textual formats can pass through firewalls and proxies between organizations without being blocked
Textual formats guarantee that numbers and binary data round-trip exactly, which partners rely on

questions.explanation: As data interchange formats, what matters is that the parties agree on the format; how pretty or efficient it is often matters little. The difficulty of getting different organizations to agree on anything outweighs most other concerns, so widely known, widely supported formats keep their place. They are not faster than binary formats, and they have known weaknesses with numbers and binary data.

questions.question: When does it make the most sense to choose a more compact or faster-to-parse format than JSON or XML?

options.text: For data used only within your own organization, especially once datasets reach terabytes
For public APIs, where many outside organizations consume the data and efficiency matters most
For small datasets, where each byte saved is a large percentage of the total size
For data exchanged once with a partner and then discarded, where readability matters least

questions.explanation: For data used only internally there is less pressure to use a lowest-common-denominator format, since only your own teams must agree on it. For a small dataset the gains are negligible, but once data reaches the terabytes the choice of format can have a big impact on storage and processing cost. Public APIs and partner exchanges are exactly where agreement and interoperability favour JSON or XML.

questions.question: Which statements about binary encodings of JSON and XML (such as MessagePack, BSON, and WBXML) are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Some extend the set of datatypes, for example distinguishing integers from floats or adding binary strings
Apart from extra datatypes, they keep the JSON or XML data model and add no schema
They are used in various niches, but none is as widely adopted as textual JSON or XML
They typically shrink a record to less than half the size of its textual JSON form

questions.explanation: Binary JSON variants (MessagePack, BSON, BJSON, UBJSON, BISON, Smile) and binary XML variants (WBXML, Fast Infoset) encode the same data model in binary. Some add datatypes such as distinct integers and floats or binary strings, but none prescribes a schema, so they must still include every field name in each record. That limits the saving: a record of 81 bytes as JSON took 66 bytes as MessagePack. They found niches, but the textual versions remain far more widely used.

optionExplanations.a: Several of these formats add types that JSON lacks, such as separate integer and floating-point types or a binary string type. That fixes some of JSON's ambiguity without changing its overall model.
optionExplanations.b: Apart from extra datatypes, these formats keep the schemaless JSON or XML data model, which is why each encoded record must still carry its field names.
optionExplanations.c: Some binary variants found useful niches, but textual JSON and XML kept broader tooling, readability, and interoperability. A modest size saving rarely outweighed that ecosystem advantage.
optionExplanations.d: Because field names are still written in every record, the saving is modest: an 81-byte JSON record became 66 bytes in MessagePack, about 18% smaller. Large reductions need schema-based formats that omit field names.

questions.question: What important size limitation is shared by schema-free binary JSON/XML variants such as MessagePack, BSON, and WBXML?

options.text: Having no schema, they must include every field name in every encoded record
They cannot represent nested objects, so deep structures must be flattened first
They lose human-readability, and that is their only significant drawback
They drop support for arrays, so repeated values need a naming convention

questions.explanation: Although these formats use binary type and length markers, they keep the schema-free JSON/XML data model. With no schema to say which field is which, every encoded record must spell out its field names (for example 'userName', 'favoriteNumber', 'interests'), which is why a record that takes 81 bytes as JSON still takes 66 bytes in MessagePack. Schema-driven formats such as Thrift, Protocol Buffers, and Avro keep names in the schema instead, so records shrink much further. They can represent nested objects and arrays, and lost readability is not their only drawback.

questions.question: MessagePack encodes a record holding userName 'Martin', favoriteNumber 1337, and interests ['daydreaming','hacking']. What does the leading byte 0x83 mean?

options.text: An object (top bits 0x80) with three fields (bottom bits 0x03)
That what follows is a string exactly three characters long
That the record was written against schema version number three
That there are 83 further bytes to read before the record ends

questions.explanation: MessagePack's `0x83` is a compact map header: the high bits identify a map/object and the low bits encode the count of three key-value fields. It describes the outer record, not the length of the following field name or a schema version.

questions.question: In MessagePack, the compact map header stores field counts from 0 to 15 in four bits. How are objects with more than 15 fields encoded?

options.text: A different type indicator, with the count in two or four bytes
The record is rejected as invalid by the encoder before it is written
The object is split into two separate objects of fifteen fields each
Field names are dropped from the encoding in order to save the space

questions.explanation: MessagePack switches from the compact fixed-map header to a wider map header whose following two or four bytes contain the element count. The 4-bit form optimizes small objects without imposing a 15-field limit.

questions.question: For a record holding userName 'Martin', favoriteNumber 1337, and interests ['daydreaming','hacking'], what are the byte counts in textual JSON and in MessagePack, and is the saving worth it?

options.text: 81 bytes versus 66 — about 18.5%, which may not be worth losing readability
81 bytes versus 32 bytes, a decisive win that justifies the loss of readability
100 bytes versus 66 bytes, a clear win that is worth the loss of readability
66 bytes versus 81 bytes, so MessagePack is actually the larger of the two

questions.explanation: A record with userName 'Martin', favoriteNumber 1337, and interests ['daydreaming','hacking'] takes 81 bytes as textual JSON with whitespace removed and 66 bytes in MessagePack, a saving of 15 bytes, about 18.5%. Such a modest reduction may not justify losing human readability and universal tooling. Schema-driven formats such as Avro shrink the same record to 32 bytes by omitting field names entirely.

questions.question: Where did Thrift and Protocol Buffers come from?

options.text: Protobuf from Google, Thrift from Facebook; both open sourced in 2007-08
Thrift came from Google and protobuf from Facebook, both open sourced in 2005
Both were developed at Apache from the start and open sourced together in 2010
Thrift came from Twitter and protobuf from LinkedIn, both open sourced in 2009

questions.explanation: Protocol Buffers originated at Google and Thrift at Facebook; both were open-sourced around 2007–2008. Their common design move is requiring a schema and replacing field names in each record with compact numeric tags.

questions.question: In a Thrift schema such as 'struct Person { 1: required string userName, 2: optional i64 favoriteNumber }', what do the numbers 1 and 2 declare?

options.text: Field tags: compact numeric aliases used in place of field names
The order in which the fields must be written into the encoded record
The byte offset at which each field begins within the encoded record
The schema version number in which each field was first introduced

questions.explanation: The numbers are field tags. Encoded records carry these compact numeric identities instead of spelling out field names, so a field can later be renamed in the schema, but a tag must never be changed or reassigned to a different meaning, because existing encoded data refers to it. They do not dictate byte offsets or record when a field was introduced.

questions.question: Which statements accurately compare Protocol Buffers and Thrift schemas? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Both identify every field by a numeric tag number declared in the schema
Marking a field required or optional, where supported, does not change its binary encoding
Protocol Buffers marks a field repeated, while Thrift has a parameterized list datatype
Protocol Buffers identifies fields by declaration order, so it needs no tag numbers

questions.explanation: Thrift and Protocol Buffers are built on the same principle: a schema in which each field has a name, a datatype, and a numeric tag, with encoded records carrying only the tags. In the schemas of the time, fields were marked required or optional; that marking only enables a runtime presence check and leaves the bytes unchanged. Protocol Buffers has no list type; instead a field is marked repeated, a third option alongside required and optional, whereas Thrift has a list datatype parameterized by element type.

optionExplanations.a: In both IDLs each field declaration includes a tag number (written '1:' in Thrift and '= 1' in Protocol Buffers). The encoded data refers to fields only by these tags, never by name.
optionExplanations.b: Required versus optional only enables a runtime check that fails if a required field is not set; nothing in the encoded bytes records whether a field was required. (Later Protocol Buffers versions dropped required altogether, which is why the claim is phrased as 'where supported'.)
optionExplanations.c: A repeated field is encoded by writing the same tag several times, which lets an optional field later become repeated. Thrift's dedicated list type does not allow that evolution but does support nested lists.
optionExplanations.d: Protocol Buffers relies on numeric field tags in both schema and encoded record; declaration order is not the field identity. Stable tags are what let readers skip unknown fields and allow fields to be reordered.

questions.question: What tooling do Thrift and Protocol Buffers provide for working with a schema, and how does application code use it?

options.text: A code generator that produces classes implementing the schema, which code calls to encode and decode records
A schema registry service that application code must query at runtime before decoding each record
A runtime interpreter that reads schema files on each call, so no classes are ever generated
A migration tool that rewrites all stored records whenever the schema definition changes

questions.explanation: Thrift and Protocol Buffers each come with a code generation tool that takes a schema definition and produces classes implementing it in various programming languages. Application code calls this generated code to encode or decode records. Code generation suits statically typed languages, giving efficient structures, compile-time type checks, and IDE autocompletion, but is less natural in dynamically typed languages.

questions.question: What is the relationship between Thrift's BinaryProtocol and CompactProtocol encodings?

options.text: Semantically equivalent; CompactProtocol packs the same tags, types, and values into fewer bytes
CompactProtocol omits the field type annotations, relying on the schema to supply each field's type
BinaryProtocol writes field names into the data, while CompactProtocol replaces them with numeric tags
CompactProtocol is lossy: it truncates large integers to fewer bytes in order to save space

questions.explanation: CompactProtocol is semantically equivalent to BinaryProtocol: both encode each field's tag, datatype, and value (with lengths where needed), and neither includes field names. CompactProtocol is smaller because it packs the field type and tag into a single byte and uses variable-length integers. A sample record took 59 bytes in BinaryProtocol and 34 in CompactProtocol. Variable-length integers are lossless; large numbers just take more bytes.

questions.question: How many bytes does Thrift's BinaryProtocol take for a record holding userName 'Martin', favoriteNumber 1337, and interests ['daydreaming','hacking'], and what annotations does each field carry?

options.text: 59 bytes, each field carrying a type annotation and, where needed, a length
34 bytes, with each field carrying only a type annotation and no length
66 bytes, because the field names are still written inline as in MessagePack
33 bytes, because integers are stored as variable-length quantities

questions.explanation: Thrift BinaryProtocol encodes a record with userName 'Martin', favoriteNumber 1337, and interests ['daydreaming','hacking'] in 59 bytes. Each field carries a type annotation and its numeric tag, and strings and lists also carry a length or element count. Because field names are replaced by tags, it is smaller than MessagePack's 66 bytes even though it uses fixed-width lengths and an eight-byte integer; CompactProtocol shrinks the same record to 34 bytes.

questions.question: What is the main reason Thrift's BinaryProtocol encodes a record more compactly than MessagePack does?

options.text: It omits field names, writing the numeric field tags from the schema in their place
It omits type annotations, because the shared schema already fixes each field's datatype
It compresses string values instead of storing them as raw UTF-8 bytes
It omits length prefixes, so the parser simply reads until the schema is satisfied

questions.explanation: MessagePack has no schema, so it must write each field name ('userName', 'favoriteNumber', 'interests') into every record. Thrift requires a schema in which each field has a tag number, so the encoded data contains just the tag numbers (1, 2, 3), which act as compact aliases for the names. Both still carry type annotations and lengths, and strings are stored as plain UTF-8. Because the data refers only to tags, tags may never be reassigned.

questions.question: Thrift's CompactProtocol encodes a record that takes 59 bytes in BinaryProtocol in only 34 bytes. Which techniques produce that reduction? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Packing the field type and tag number into a single byte
Variable-length integers, so 1337 takes two bytes instead of eight
Dropping type annotations, since the schema records each field's type
Compressing string values with gzip before writing them

questions.explanation: CompactProtocol is semantically equivalent to BinaryProtocol; it just packs the same information more tightly. It combines field type and tag number in one byte and encodes integers with a variable number of bytes, using the top bit of each byte to say whether more bytes follow. So 1337 needs two bytes rather than a fixed eight. Type information is kept, because readers need it to skip fields they don't recognize.

optionExplanations.a: When a small field tag is used, CompactProtocol combines the tag and type code in one byte instead of writing them separately. This saves bytes while still letting a reader identify and skip the field.
optionExplanations.b: Variable-length integers spend fewer bytes on small magnitudes, and a continuation bit in each byte indicates whether more follow. Thus 1337 needs two bytes instead of a fixed eight-byte slot.
optionExplanations.c: CompactProtocol still carries type information because readers need it to parse and skip fields they may not recognize. The schema alone is insufficient when old code encounters a new tag.
optionExplanations.d: Strings are still stored as UTF-8 bytes with a length prefix; no general-purpose compression is applied. The reduction comes from tighter field headers and variable-length integers.

questions.question: With Thrift CompactProtocol's signed variable-length integers, which ranges fit in one and two bytes?

options.text: -64 to 63 in one byte, -8192 to 8191 in two, more bytes for bigger numbers
Numbers from 0 to 255 fit in one byte, and 0 to 65535 fit in two bytes
Numbers from -128 to 127 fit in one byte, and -32768 to 32767 in two bytes
All integers occupy exactly four bytes, whatever their magnitude

questions.explanation: After signed values are mapped with zigzag encoding, each byte contributes seven payload bits and one continuation bit. One byte represents −64 through 63; two represent −8192 through 8191. Larger magnitudes consume additional bytes.

questions.question: How does Protocol Buffers' encoding of a record holding userName 'Martin', favoriteNumber 1337, and interests ['daydreaming','hacking'] compare with Thrift's CompactProtocol?

options.text: One format, packing bits slightly differently; 33 bytes, one fewer than Thrift
Protobuf takes 59 bytes, exactly matching Thrift's BinaryProtocol encoding
Protobuf takes 66 bytes, exactly matching the size of the MessagePack encoding
Protobuf has three binary formats and takes 34 bytes in its most compact one

questions.explanation: Protocol Buffers has only one binary encoding format. It packs bits slightly differently from Thrift's CompactProtocol but uses the same ideas (field tags combined with type codes, variable-length integers), and it fits the sample record in 33 bytes versus CompactProtocol's 34. The two are essentially tied; both are far smaller than MessagePack (66 bytes) because they omit field names.

questions.question: In Thrift and Protocol Buffers, what do `required` and `optional` change in the binary encoding?

options.text: Nothing in the encoding; required only enables a runtime check
Required fields are encoded without a tag, saving a byte
Required fields are written first in the byte stream
Required fields are validated by the schema registry at write time

questions.explanation: They do not change the wire representation. `required` adds a runtime validation check that the field is present, which can catch bugs but makes future removal unsafe; optionality is therefore an evolution constraint rather than a byte-level optimization.

questions.question: In Thrift and Protocol Buffers schemas, which part of a field's definition can be changed safely, and which must never change?

options.text: Names can change, since the data refers to tags; tags cannot change
You may change a field's tag freely but never its name, which the data refers to
You may change both names and tags freely, since the schema travels with the data
You may change neither, because both are written into every encoded record

questions.explanation: Schema evolution means changing a schema over time while old and new code keep exchanging data. In Thrift and Protocol Buffers an encoded record identifies each field only by its numeric tag and datatype. Field names may therefore change, since encoded data never refers to them, but changing a field's tag would make all existing encoded data invalid or misinterpreted.

questions.question: In Thrift or Protocol Buffers, old code reads a record written by new code that includes a field with a tag number the old code has never seen. How does the old code cope?

options.text: It ignores the field, using the field's datatype annotation to work out how many bytes to skip
It looks up the new field's name, which is written into the record, and adds it to its object
It fails to decode the record, so every reader must be upgraded before any writer adds a field
It substitutes the default value declared for that tag in its own copy of the schema

questions.explanation: Each encoded field carries its tag number and a datatype annotation. When old code meets a tag it doesn't recognize, it can simply ignore that field, and the datatype annotation tells the parser how many bytes to skip. This is what gives forward compatibility when fields are added, provided each new field gets a new tag number. Field names are not in the data, and the old schema has no entry, let alone a default, for the new tag.

questions.question: In Thrift or Protocol Buffers, why must a field added after a schema's initial deployment be optional or have a default value?

options.text: New code reading records written before the field existed would fail the required check
Old code would otherwise crash when it meets the unknown tag, so the field must be optional to be skipped
Required fields take extra bytes in the encoding, which would make the new records incompatible in size
Required fields may only use tag numbers assigned in the first version of the schema

questions.explanation: As long as each field has a unique tag, new code can always read old data, because tags keep their meaning. But old records were written before the new field existed, so they don't contain it. If the new field were required, the runtime check would fail whenever new code read old data, breaking backward compatibility. Old code skipping an unknown tag is a separate, forward-compatibility matter, and required versus optional does not change the encoded bytes.

questions.question: In Thrift and Protocol Buffers, which rules apply when removing a field from a schema? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Removal is like addition, with the backward and forward compatibility concerns reversed
Only an optional field can be removed; a required field can never be removed
The removed field's tag number must never be reused for another field
The removed field must be renamed to mark it deprecated, so old readers know to skip it

questions.explanation: Removing a field reverses the concerns of adding one: old readers now see new data that lacks the field, and new readers see old data that still contains it. So only an optional field can be removed (old code that required it would reject new data), and its tag number must be permanently retired, because old data containing that tag may still exist and new code must ignore it rather than misinterpret it.

optionExplanations.a: Removing a field reverses addition's compatibility directions: new readers see old data containing an extra tag, while old readers see new data missing a field. Both cases must be tolerated.
optionExplanations.b: If an old reader requires the removed field, new records without it cannot be decoded as expected. Only optional fields can disappear without violating that reader contract.
optionExplanations.c: Historical records may still contain the retired tag, so assigning it a new meaning would make new readers misinterpret old bytes. The number must remain permanently reserved.
optionExplanations.d: Field names are not carried in these tagged binary records, and renaming does not teach old readers to skip anything. Compatibility depends on optionality and stable numeric tags.

questions.question: In Thrift or Protocol Buffers, what happens when a field changes from a 32-bit to a 64-bit integer?

options.text: Possible but risky: new reading old is fine, old reading new can truncate
Both directions are always safe, since integers are variable-length
New code reading old data truncates; old code reading new data is safe
Only widening conversions work, so a 32-bit field must be replaced by a new field

questions.explanation: A new reader can decode old 32-bit values into a wider variable, so backward reading is safe. An old reader may truncate a new value that exceeds 32 bits, so forward compatibility is conditional rather than guaranteed. The byte encoding alone cannot protect the narrower application variable.

questions.question: Protocol Buffers has no list datatype; instead a field can be marked repeated. How is a repeated field encoded, and what schema change does that allow?

options.text: The same tag appears once per value, so an optional field can later become repeated
A length-prefixed array holds all values, so an optional field can never be changed to repeated
It is encoded exactly like Thrift's parameterized list type, so it also supports nested lists
All values are concatenated into one field, so old readers see them merged into a single value

questions.explanation: Protocol Buffers represents a repeated field by writing the same field tag multiple times, one value per occurrence. That lets a single-valued optional field evolve into a repeated one: new code reading old data sees a list of zero or one elements, and old code reading new data sees only the last element. Thrift instead has a dedicated list datatype, which doesn't allow this evolution but does support nested lists.

questions.question: Why was Apache Avro created?

options.text: Started in 2009 as a Hadoop subproject, because Thrift didn't fit Hadoop's needs
Started at Google in 2007 as an intended successor to Protocol Buffers
Started at Facebook in 2009 as an intended successor to Apache Thrift
Standardized in 1984 as part of the ASN.1 family of schema languages

questions.explanation: Avro was started in 2009 as a subproject of Hadoop, because Thrift was not a good fit for Hadoop's use cases. Its design differs from Thrift and Protocol Buffers: there are no tag numbers, and data is decoded by resolving the writer's schema against the reader's schema by field name. That makes Avro friendlier to schemas generated automatically, for example from database tables, which is a common need in Hadoop-style data processing.

questions.question: Avro has two schema languages. What are they for?

options.text: Avro IDL for humans, and a JSON-based one for machines
One for reading and one for writing
One for statically typed and one for dynamically typed languages
One for records and one for unions

questions.explanation: Avro IDL is concise and convenient for people to write, while the JSON representation is convenient for programs to generate and consume. Both describe the same record, field, union, and type information; they are alternate syntaxes, not separate read and write schemas.

questions.question: What does an Avro schema lack that Thrift and Protocol Buffers schemas have?

options.text: Field tag numbers
Field names
Field datatypes
Default values

questions.explanation: Avro schemas have field names, datatypes, and defaults, but no tag numbers. Because nothing in the encoded data identifies fields, Avro decodes by walking the writer's schema in order and matches fields to the reader's schema by name. This makes Avro's binary encoding very compact and makes it easy to generate schemas automatically, but the reader must know the exact writer's schema.

questions.question: How many bytes does Avro take for a record holding userName 'Martin', favoriteNumber 1337, and interests ['daydreaming','hacking'], and how does that rank against the other binary encodings?

options.text: 32 bytes, smaller than Protobuf and Thrift
33 bytes, tied with Protocol Buffers
34 bytes, tied with Thrift CompactProtocol
59 bytes, the least compact binary format

questions.explanation: Avro encodes the record in just 32 bytes, the most compact of the binary encodings compared: Protocol Buffers took 33, Thrift CompactProtocol 34, Thrift BinaryProtocol 59, and MessagePack 66, against 81 bytes of textual JSON. Avro saves space because the encoded data contains only values, with no field tags or type annotations; the writer's schema supplies field order and types.

questions.question: What information lets an Avro reader parse a raw encoded record?

options.text: The writer's schema supplies field order and types
Every value carries its own field tag and type marker
The reader searches the bytes for embedded field names
The reader schema must be byte-identical to the writer schema

questions.explanation: Avro minimizes record overhead by omitting tags and type annotations: the writer's schema determines the sequence and encoding. A reader obtains that writer schema and resolves it against its own schema, matching fields by name and applying defaults or conversions where permitted.

questions.question: In Avro, what are the writer's schema and the reader's schema?

options.text: Writer's schema: the version the encoder knows. Reader's: the version the decoder expects
The writer's schema is stored in the database; the reader's schema is negotiated at runtime
They are two names for the same schema, viewed from the encoder's and decoder's side respectively
The writer's schema is always the newest version deployed and the reader's always the oldest

questions.explanation: The writer's schema is whatever schema version the encoding application knows, for example compiled into it, and is used to encode the data. The reader's schema is the version the decoding application expects and its code relies on. They are separate artifacts that can be different versions, possibly written years apart, which is why Avro resolves one against the other when decoding.

questions.question: In Avro, how must the writer's schema and the reader's schema relate to each other for decoding to work?

options.text: They need only be compatible; the library resolves their differences when decoding
They must be byte-identical, which the library verifies by comparing schema hashes
The reader must always hold the newer schema and upgrade data to it before decoding
The writer must embed both schemas in every record so the reader can compare them

questions.explanation: The key idea in Avro is that writer and reader schemas don't have to be the same; they only need to be compatible. When data is read, the Avro library looks at both schemas side by side and translates data from the writer's schema into the reader's: it matches fields by name, ignores fields the reader doesn't know, fills in defaults for fields the writer didn't have, and performs supported type conversions.

questions.question: When Avro decodes data, which rules apply when resolving the writer's schema against the reader's schema? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Fields may appear in a different order, because resolution matches fields by name
A field in the writer's schema but not in the reader's schema is ignored
A field in the reader's schema but not the writer's gets the reader's declared default
Any difference in a field's type makes the reader reject the record

questions.explanation: Avro resolves by field name rather than position: field order may differ, writer-only fields are ignored, and reader-only fields receive the default declared in the reader's schema. A type difference is not automatically an error, because changing a field's datatype is allowed when Avro can convert the type.

optionExplanations.a: Avro compares schemas by field name, so declaration order can differ without changing meaning. The writer's schema supplies byte order while resolution maps values into reader fields.
optionExplanations.b: A writer-only field has no destination in the reader's expected object, so Avro can consume and ignore it using the writer's schema. This supports old readers encountering newer data.
optionExplanations.c: A reader-only field has no bytes in the old record, so its declared default supplies a value. This is the mechanism for new readers to consume older data.
optionExplanations.d: Avro permits type changes it can convert, such as int to long, so not every type difference is fatal. Truly incompatible types do fail, but the option states the rule too absolutely.

questions.question: In Avro's writer/reader terms, what do forward and backward compatibility mean?

options.text: Forward: new writer's schema, old reader's schema. Backward: new reader's schema, old writer's schema
Forward: new reader's schema, old writer's schema. Backward: new writer's schema, old reader's schema
Both terms require the reader's schema to be the newer of the two versions involved
Both terms require the writer's schema to be the newer of the two versions involved

questions.explanation: Forward compatibility means old code can read new data: in Avro, a new version of the schema as writer and an old version as reader. Backward compatibility means new code can read old data: a new schema as reader and an old schema as writer. In the forward case the reader is old; in the backward case the reader is new.

questions.question: In Avro, which fields can be added to or removed from a schema while keeping both backward and forward compatibility?

options.text: Only fields that have a default value
Only fields placed at the end of the record
Any field, since fields are matched by name
Only fields whose type is a union that includes null

questions.explanation: To maintain compatibility, you may only add or remove a field that has a default value. If you add a field without a default, a new reader reading old data has nothing to fill in, breaking backward compatibility; if you remove a field without a default, an old reader reading new data has nothing to fill in, breaking forward compatibility. Matching by name handles order, not missing values. A union with null makes null a legal value, but it is the declared default (such as null) that makes the field safe to add or remove.

questions.question: Which mistake breaks which compatibility direction in Avro?

options.text: Adding without a default breaks backward; removing without one breaks forward
Adding breaks forward compatibility; removing breaks backward compatibility
Both mistakes break backward compatibility only
Avro matches fields by name rather than by tag, so neither of these changes affects compatibility

questions.explanation: A new reader processing old data will not find an added field, so the reader schema needs a default for backward compatibility. An old reader processing new data expects a removed field, so keeping a default for that field preserves forward compatibility.

questions.question: How does Avro treat null, and what is the restriction?

options.text: null needs an explicit union branch; it cannot be a default otherwise
null is a valid default for every field, as in most languages
Avro rejects null outright, so an absent value has to be encoded as an empty string instead
null requires a separate nullable marker on each field

questions.explanation: Avro represents nullability explicitly as a union containing `null`; a field cannot simply use null as its default if null is absent from its type. The extra declaration prevents callers from silently treating every value as nullable, reducing an important class of mistakes.

questions.question: Avro has no required and optional field markers like Protocol Buffers and Thrift. What does it use instead?

options.text: Union types (for example a union with null) and default values
Numeric field tags combined with per-record presence bits
A nullable keyword applied to each field that may be absent
Every field is implicitly required, so all fields must always be written

questions.explanation: Avro expresses optionality differently: a field that may be null is declared with a union type that includes null, and a field that may be missing from older data gets a default value. For example, 'union { null, long } favoriteNumber = null' makes the field nullable with a default of null. So Avro has the capability, but not through required and optional markers.

questions.question: In Avro, what is the compatibility of changing a field's datatype, renaming a field (using aliases in the reader's schema), and adding a branch to a union type?

options.text: Datatype changes if convertible; renames and new union branches are backward-only
All three changes are both backward and forward compatible
Renaming and adding a union branch are forward compatible but not backward compatible
All three changes are rejected by Avro's schema resolution rules

questions.explanation: Avro may change a datatype when it defines a conversion. A new reader can recognize an old field name through aliases, making a rename backward- but not forward-compatible. Adding a union branch has the same asymmetry because only the new reader knows the additional branch.

questions.question: Why doesn't Avro simply include the full writer's schema with every encoded record?

options.text: Because the schema would dwarf the record, wasting the binary saving
Because a schema cannot itself be serialized into the container format
Because the reader has no way to parse a schema definition at runtime
Because the Avro specification explicitly forbids embedding the schema

questions.explanation: Avro records can be very small because they omit field names and type tags. Repeating a full schema with every record would often cost more than the data itself and destroy that compactness. Instead the writer's schema is stored once per file, referenced by a version number per record, or negotiated once per connection.

questions.question: How can an Avro reader find out which writer's schema encoded the data in each of these settings? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A large file of records: the writer's schema is stored once at the start of the file
A database of individually written records: each record starts with a schema version number
A bidirectional network connection: the peers negotiate the schema version at connection setup
Any setting: the reader infers the writer's schema from the record's byte patterns

questions.explanation: How the reader gets the writer's schema depends on context. An object container file holding millions of records with the same schema stores that schema once at the beginning. In a database, records are written at different times under different schemas, so each record can start with a version number that the reader looks up in a stored list of schema versions (LinkedIn's Espresso works this way). Over a bidirectional connection, as in Avro RPC, the peers negotiate the schema once and use it for the whole connection.

optionExplanations.a: An Avro object container file stores the writer's schema once in its header and applies it to all the records that follow. Repeating the schema per compact record would waste space.
optionExplanations.b: Individually stored database records may come from many application versions, so a small version number points into a list of schemas kept in the database. The reader fetches that exact writer's schema before decoding.
optionExplanations.c: Two endpoints on a bidirectional Avro RPC connection can negotiate the schema version during setup and reuse it for the connection's lifetime. Per-message repetition is unnecessary.
optionExplanations.d: Avro data carries no field tags or type markers, so the same bytes could be a string, an integer, or something else. Without the writer's schema the reader cannot even tell where one value ends and the next begins.

questions.question: Beyond decoding, what does a database of schema versions give you?

options.text: It documents the data and allows compatibility to be checked
It enables the database to migrate stored records automatically
It provides the key rotation needed to re-encrypt older records
It allows obsolete schema versions to be deleted without risk

questions.explanation: A schema registry is also authoritative documentation: decoding depends on it, so it cannot silently drift from reality. It can validate proposed changes for forward and backward compatibility before producers or consumers are deployed.

questions.question: When dumping a relational database to Avro files, what advantage comes from Avro having no field tag numbers?

options.text: Avro suits generated schemas: regenerate from the table and export, since fields match by name
Avro can infer the schema at read time, so no schema is needed for the dump at all
Avro stores the column names inside every record, which makes schemas unnecessary
Avro requires tags to be assigned by hand, which is what makes dumps reproducible

questions.explanation: An Avro schema can be generated from the relational schema: a record schema per table, with one field per column, named after the column. If the database schema changes, the export just generates a new Avro schema and writes data with it. Readers match fields by name, so the updated writer's schema can still be resolved against an older reader's schema. No tag numbers need to be assigned or tracked between runs.

questions.question: When generating a binary dump from a changing relational schema, what extra tag-management work would Thrift or Protocol Buffers require compared with Avro?

options.text: Someone must map columns to tags by hand, taking care never to reuse old tags
None; Thrift and Protocol Buffers handle dynamically generated schemas exactly as Avro does
None; tags can always be derived from column order, which never changes between dumps
Each row would need its own schema, since tags cannot be shared between rows of a table

questions.explanation: With Thrift or Protocol Buffers, every time the database schema changes someone would have to update the mapping from column names to field tags, and an automated generator would have to be careful never to assign a previously used tag. Column order is not stable, since columns are added and removed. Avro matches fields by name, so a regenerated schema works without bookkeeping; dynamically generated schemas were a design goal of Avro but not of the tag-based formats.

questions.question: Which statements about generating code from a schema (as Thrift and Protocol Buffers do, and Avro optionally does) are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Static languages gain efficient objects, type checks, and IDE completion
Dynamic languages gain little without compile-time type checking
Generated code can obstruct runtime schemas and build-free workflows
Every language requires generated classes before Avro can decode data

questions.explanation: Generated classes give statically typed languages efficient domain objects, compile-time type checks, and IDE completion. Dynamic languages gain less because they lack compile-time checking, often avoid a build step, and may receive schemas generated at runtime; Avro therefore supports generic decoding without mandatory code generation.

optionExplanations.a: Generated classes map schema fields into efficient native objects while the compiler catches wrong types and IDEs offer completion. These benefits align with statically typed development.
optionExplanations.b: Dynamic languages do not need generated declarations to satisfy a compiler, so generic dictionaries or objects can expose decoded fields naturally. Generated wrappers add less safety value.
optionExplanations.c: When schemas arrive at runtime, pre-generating a class for every shape is impossible or delays access behind another build step. Generic decoding preserves the dynamic workflow.
optionExplanations.d: Avro supports generic readers that interpret a writer schema without generated application classes. Code generation is a convenience for typed code, not a decoding requirement in every language.

questions.question: How can an Avro object container file be decoded without generated classes?

options.text: The container header gives a generic decoder the writer's schema
Every individual Avro record repeats all field names
The decoder guesses the schema from byte patterns
Generated code is secretly downloaded from the registry

questions.explanation: Self-description exists at the container-file level, not necessarily in every raw Avro record. A generic decoder reads the header's writer schema and then interprets each compact record without generated application classes.

questions.question: How do the schema languages of Protocol Buffers, Thrift and Avro compare to XML Schema and JSON Schema?

options.text: Much simpler, without the detailed validation rules of XML or JSON Schema
They are more complex, supporting richer validation than XML or JSON Schema
They are exactly equivalent in expressiveness to XML Schema and JSON Schema
They support no validation whatsoever, unlike XML Schema and JSON Schema

questions.explanation: Protocol Buffers, Thrift, and Avro focus on describing data needed for interoperable binary encoding, so their schemas omit many rich validation constraints found in XML Schema or JSON Schema. That smaller scope makes implementations simpler and encourages broader language support.

questions.question: What is ASN.1, and where is it still in use today?

options.text: A 1984 schema language whose DER encoding still carries X.509 certificates
ASN.1 dates from 1994 and is no longer used in any protocol still in service
ASN.1 resolves fields by name as Avro does, and is recommended for new work
ASN.1 is a textual format that was superseded by XML in the early 2000s

questions.explanation: ASN.1 is a schema language standardized in 1984. Its DER binary encoding remains widely used for X.509 certificates, and it supports tag-based evolution, but its complexity and documentation make it an unattractive default for new application formats.

questions.question: How does an application typically exchange queries and results with a relational database over the network?

options.text: A database-specific binary protocol, decoded by the vendor's driver (ODBC or JDBC)
A standard SQL-over-HTTP protocol that all relational database vendors share
Protocol Buffers messages, adopted by all major relational databases as their wire format
JSON documents that the application parses itself after receiving each response

questions.explanation: Many data systems use their own proprietary binary encoding. Most relational databases have a network protocol for sending queries and receiving responses that is specific to that database. The vendor provides a driver, used through APIs such as ODBC or JDBC, that decodes responses from the protocol into in-memory data structures, so applications rarely see the bytes.

questions.question: Which advantages do schema-driven binary encodings have? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They omit repeated field names and can be much more compact than binary JSON variants
The required schema is reliable, machine-checkable documentation
A schema registry can check compatibility before deployment, and generated classes can provide compile-time type checking in statically typed languages
They infer a schema independently from every record, so producers and consumers never exchange schema information

questions.explanation: The schema supplies four distinct benefits: compact bytes, documentation that cannot drift from the decoder, pre-deployment forward/backward compatibility checks, and generated types for statically typed code. Dynamic languages may choose generic decoding instead of code generation.

optionExplanations.a: The shared schema supplies field names and types out of band, so each record can encode compact tags or only ordered values. Binary JSON must often repeat field-name strings because it lacks that schema.
optionExplanations.b: A required schema is parsed by the same tools that encode and decode records, so it cannot silently drift into an entirely aspirational document. It serves as executable, machine-checkable documentation.
optionExplanations.c: A registry can compare proposed and existing schemas before rollout, while generated typed classes move some mistakes to compilation. These checks catch compatibility problems earlier than production decoding.
optionExplanations.d: Schema-driven formats do not infer a complete independent schema from every record; writer and reader must obtain compatible schema definitions through code, a file header, a registry, or negotiation.

questions.question: How do schema-based binary encodings compare with schemaless databases for flexibility?

options.text: Evolution rules can offer comparable flexibility plus explicit checks
Schemas freeze the structure, so any change requires rewriting all stored data
Comparable flexibility, but weaker guarantees, since a schema can drift from the data
Schemaless storage is more flexible, since schema formats permit only appending fields

questions.explanation: A declared schema does not imply a frozen structure. Optional fields, defaults, stable tags, and writer/reader schema resolution allow compatible change over time, giving the same kind of flexibility as schema-on-read JSON databases while making compatibility explicit and checkable. Old records need not be rewritten: readers resolve them with defaults. Fields can be added anywhere (by new tag or by name), not only at the end. And because the schema is required for decoding, it cannot silently drift from the data the way hand-written documentation can, so the guarantees are better, not weaker.

questions.question: What is compatibility a property of?

options.text: It is a relationship between the encoding process and the decoding process
Compatibility is a property of one schema version considered on its own
Compatibility is a property of the encoding library rather than the data
Compatibility is a property of the deployment process, not of the encoding

questions.explanation: Compatibility describes whether data produced by one encoding process can be consumed by another decoding process. The relationship matters wherever data crosses time or process boundaries: stored database records, service calls, and asynchronous messages.

questions.question: One application stores data in a database, and a later version of the same application reads it back. Which compatibility does this require, and why?

options.text: Backward: storing data is like sending a message to your future self, which must decode what older code wrote
Forward: the earlier version that writes the data must anticipate the schema of the later reader
Neither: both reader and writer belong to the same application, so the data format cannot differ
Only forward: the database automatically stores data in the format of the newest code version

questions.explanation: In a database, the process that writes encodes the data and the process that reads decodes it. When the reader is just a later version of the same process, storing something is like sending a message to your future self. Backward compatibility (newer code reading data written by older code) is clearly necessary, otherwise the future version can't decode what was previously written. The database does not re-encode data to match new code.

questions.question: Why do databases often need forward compatibility, not just backward compatibility?

options.text: Several processes, some running newer code and some older, access the same database at the same time
Each deployment requires new code to read the data that older code wrote before the upgrade
A schema migration rewrites every row into the new format before any new code is started
Forward compatibility is not needed, since a database is read only by the newest deployed code

questions.explanation: It is common for several processes, different services or several instances of one service, to access a database at once.
