During a rolling upgrade some instances run new code and some still run old code, so a value may be written by newer code and then read by older code. Old code reading new data is forward compatibility. New code reading old data is the backward direction, which databases also need.

questions.question: During a rolling database upgrade, what additional read-modify-write hazard can make an old application version erase a field introduced by new code?

options.text: Old code decodes the record, changes it, and re-encodes it without the new field it didn't know about
The old code crashes as soon as it encounters a field it does not recognize in the record
The database rejects the old code's write in order to protect the field added by the new code
The unknown field is silently renamed so that the record still matches the old schema

questions.explanation: Suppose new code adds a field and writes a value for it. Old code, which doesn't know the field, then reads the record, updates another field, and writes it back. If the old code decoded the record into objects that have no place for the unknown field, re-encoding drops it and the new data is silently lost. The desirable behaviour is for old code to keep the new field intact even though it can't interpret it.

questions.question: Thrift, Protocol Buffers, and Avro can preserve fields a reader does not recognize. How can a new field still be lost when old application code updates a record?

options.text: Old code's model objects lack the field, so re-encoding drops it
The wire encoding always destroys every field the reader does not understand
The database engine removes them while acquiring a central write lock
A network retry deletes fields whose update is not idempotent

questions.explanation: The encoding formats support preserving unknown fields, but care is still needed at the application level. If old code decodes a stored value into its own model objects, which have no slot for the new field, and later re-encodes those objects, the unknown field is lost in that translation. The fix belongs in the mapping and update path: carry unknown fields through, or update only the fields that changed.

questions.question: How old can coexisting values in one long-lived database be?

options.text: Some may be milliseconds old while others are years old
Nightly rewriting limits every value to less than one day
Automatic expiration limits every value to ninety days
Their ages differ only by the current replication lag

questions.explanation: Application code may be replaced quickly, but stored records can survive for years. A database can therefore mix very recent values with values encoded by much older software, making backward compatibility a continuing requirement rather than a one-time migration concern.

questions.question: Why does a database keep holding data in old encodings long after every application server runs new code?

options.text: Code is replaced within minutes, but stored data keeps its original encoding unless explicitly rewritten
Databases refuse to accept data in a new encoding until every server has been upgraded
Old encodings are smaller, so databases keep them in preference to newer ones
Each deployment rewrites all data, but replicas lag behind and keep the old copies

questions.explanation: A new version of a server-side application can replace the old one within a few minutes, but database contents don't change with it: data written five years ago is still there in its original encoding unless it has been rewritten since. This is summed up as 'data outlives code'. A single database may contain values written milliseconds ago alongside values written years ago, so readers must keep handling old encodings.

questions.question: How expensive is migrating data into a new schema, and what cheap alternative do relational databases offer?

options.text: Expensive on large datasets; adding a column with a null default needs no rewrite
Cheap, because databases rewrite rows lazily in the background as each row is next read
Expensive, so relational databases forbid adding columns once a table holds data
Cheap, since only the table's indexes must be rebuilt, not the rows themselves

questions.explanation: Rewriting (migrating) every stored record into a new schema is possible but expensive on a large dataset, so most databases avoid it. Most relational databases allow simple changes, such as adding a column with a null default, without rewriting existing data: when an old row is read, the database fills in null for columns missing from the stored data. Nothing rewrites rows lazily or merely rebuilds indexes in this case; the old rows simply stay in their original encoding. MySQL is a notable exception that often rewrites the whole table even when it is not strictly necessary.

questions.question: How can schema evolution make a database whose records were written under many schema versions appear to use a single schema?

options.text: Each record is decoded with its writer's schema and resolved into the reader's schema
Every stored record is rewritten whenever the application's schema definition changes
Only one writer's schema is permitted in the database at a time, enforced on every write
All records are converted to untyped JSON before any application is allowed to read them

questions.explanation: Each stored record is linked to the writer's schema it was encoded with, for example by a schema version number at the start of the record. On read, the record is decoded with that writer's schema and translated into the reader's current schema: fields the reader doesn't know are ignored, missing fields get the reader's defaults, and renamed fields can be matched through aliases. The database therefore appears to have one schema even though storage holds records from many historical versions, and nothing has to be rewritten. LinkedIn's document database Espresso works this way, using Avro for storage.

questions.question: Which schema should a batch archival export normally use?

options.text: The latest schema at export time
The oldest schema ever deployed
A separate inline schema per record
The schema of the most recently written source record

questions.explanation: An archival snapshot is immutable and written as a batch, so it can normalize all records to the latest schema during export. One schema for the whole file makes Avro containers and columnar formats compact and easy to decode later.

questions.question: In network communication between processes, what is meant by a 'service'?

options.text: The API a server exposes over the network for clients to call
Any process that both sends and receives messages as an equal peer of others
A named topic on a message broker to which consumer processes subscribe
A database table that client processes read from and write to directly

questions.explanation: The most common way to arrange network communication is with two roles: servers expose an API over the network, and clients connect to make requests to it. The API a server exposes is called a service. The web works this way: browsers request HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images from web servers and submit data with POST requests, using standardized protocols and formats. A service differs from a database because it exposes only operations defined by its own application logic.

questions.question: When client-side JavaScript in a browser requests data from a server (the Ajax technique), how does the server's response typically differ from an ordinary web page?

options.text: It is data in an encoding convenient for the client code, such as JSON, rather than HTML for display
It is always HTML, which the script inserts into the page exactly as received from the server
It is a binary Protocol Buffers message, since HTTP requires binary payloads for scripts
It is a SOAP envelope, since Ajax requests can only carry XML documents

questions.explanation: A client-side JavaScript application can use XMLHttpRequest to act as an HTTP client. The server's response is then typically not HTML for a human to read but data in an encoding convenient for further processing by the client code, such as JSON. HTTP is only the transport; the API on top is application-specific, so client and server must agree on its details. Native mobile and desktop apps call servers the same way.

questions.question: What is the name for the architectural style in which a large application is decomposed into smaller services by area of functionality, with one service calling another as a client when it needs that service's data?

options.text: Service-oriented architecture (SOA), more recently refined as microservices
N-tier architecture, where each tier only calls the tier directly below it
Peer-to-peer architecture, where every node holds a full copy of all data
Shared-database integration, where services coordinate through common tables

questions.explanation: A server can itself be a client of another service; a typical web app server is a client of a database. Decomposing a large application into smaller services by area of functionality, each requesting functionality or data from the others, has traditionally been called service-oriented architecture (SOA), and more recently refined and rebranded as microservices. A key goal is that each service can be deployed and evolved independently, so services communicate through APIs rather than shared tables.

questions.question: How does the interface a service offers its clients differ from the interface a database offers?

options.text: A service exposes an application-specific API fixed by its business logic; a database allows arbitrary queries
A service allows arbitrary queries over its data, whereas a database restricts clients to predefined operations
The two interfaces are identical; they differ only in how durably they store the submitted data
A service only stores data, while a database only computes results over data passed to it by clients

questions.explanation: Services resemble databases in that clients submit and query data. But a database allows arbitrary queries in a general query language, whereas a service exposes an application-specific API that only allows inputs and outputs predetermined by its business logic. That restriction gives encapsulation: the service can impose fine-grained limits on what clients can and cannot do and can change its internals without breaking them.

questions.question: What is the key design goal of a service-oriented or microservices architecture?

options.text: To let each team deploy and evolve its own service independently
To maximize raw performance by moving every service onto a binary encoding
To minimize the number of services by consolidating teams around one codebase
To enforce one shared schema across every service so encodings always match

questions.explanation: A key design goal of SOA and microservices is to make an application easier to change and maintain by making services independently deployable and evolvable: each service is owned by one team that can release new versions frequently without coordinating with other teams. The consequence is that old and new versions of servers and clients run at the same time, so the data encoding they use must stay compatible across versions of the service API.

questions.question: Why is “web service” a slight misnomer?

options.text: HTTP services are also used by native apps and between backends
The term describes only browser front ends, not server endpoints
Every web service must use SOAP rather than ordinary HTTP
Every web service must use REST with GET, POST, and PUT

questions.explanation: The name is a slight misnomer because HTTP services also connect native apps, internal microservices, and different organizations' backend systems. Those contexts differ in trust, deployment coordination, and compatibility obligations even though all use HTTP.

questions.question: What is REST?

options.text: Not a protocol but a design philosophy built on HTTP principles
REST is a protocol standardized by the W3C and layered on top of SOAP
REST is an encoding format based on JSON
REST is an RPC framework using HTTP as transport

questions.explanation: REST is an architectural style, not a protocol or encoding. It builds on HTTP concepts such as resources, URLs, methods, caching, and content types; an API following those principles is described as RESTful.

questions.question: Which statements about SOAP's Web Services Description Language (WSDL) and its consequences are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: WSDL describes SOAP services and can generate typed client code
SOAP and WSDL complexity makes tooling and IDE support important
Unsupported languages and vendor interoperability can be difficult
WSDL displaced REST for nearly all modern public APIs

questions.explanation: SOAP is an XML-based protocol for network API requests, and a SOAP service's API is described in WSDL. WSDL enables code generation so a client can call a remote service through local classes and methods. Because WSDL is not designed to be human-readable and SOAP messages are hard to build by hand, users rely heavily on tool support and IDEs; languages without vendor support struggle, and vendors' implementations often interoperate poorly. SOAP remains in many large enterprises but fell out of favour elsewhere, while REST became predominant for public APIs.

optionExplanations.a: WSDL is a machine-readable contract for SOAP operations and message structures. Tools can turn that contract into local-looking typed client classes and method calls.
optionExplanations.b: SOAP envelopes, extensions, and WSDL contracts are difficult to construct and inspect manually, so users depend heavily on generators, IDEs, and vendor tooling. The abstraction brings operational complexity.
optionExplanations.c: A language outside a vendor's supported toolchain may struggle to consume the contract, and nominally standardized SOAP stacks have had interoperability differences. Standards do not guarantee identical implementations.
optionExplanations.d: REST became the predominant public-API style in many ecosystems, while SOAP remained common in some enterprises. WSDL did not displace REST across nearly all modern APIs.

questions.question: Match each of these earlier remote-call technologies (EJB, Java RMI, DCOM, CORBA) to its main defect.

options.text: EJB and RMI are Java-only, DCOM is Microsoft-only, and CORBA is excessively complex
EJB is Microsoft-only, DCOM is Java-only, and CORBA is criticized for being too simple
All four are limited to the Java platform, which is why none of them saw wide adoption
All four provide full backward and forward compatibility but have poor performance

questions.explanation: Enterprise JavaBeans and Java's Remote Method Invocation are limited to Java; DCOM is limited to Microsoft platforms; CORBA is excessively complex and does not provide backward or forward compatibility. All are based on remote procedure calls, and their history illustrates that making remote calls resemble local methods does not remove network and compatibility constraints.

questions.question: When does the RPC idea date from, what does it try to do, and is the attempt sound?

options.text: Since the 1970s; it seeks location transparency, a fundamentally flawed aim
Since the 1990s; it seeks location transparency, and the abstraction holds up
Since the 1970s; it seeks protocol transparency, which is largely harmless
Since 2000; it seeks network transparency, and is the future of service calls

questions.explanation: RPC dates to the 1970s and tries to provide location transparency by making a network call look like a local function call. The abstraction is fundamentally leaky because networks add partial failure, variable latency, serialization, retries, and uncertainty that local calls do not have.

questions.question: How does a network request differ from a local function call? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The request or response can be lost, or the remote machine slow or down, for reasons outside the caller's control
A request can time out with no result, leaving the caller unable to tell whether it was executed
Retrying a request whose response was lost may perform the action twice unless the protocol deduplicates
Its latency is higher but fixed and predictable, so a timeout can be chosen exactly

questions.explanation: Unlike a local call, a network request can be lost, delayed, duplicated by a retry, or processed even when its response never arrives. Parameters must be encoded into bytes and translated across language type systems. Latency ranges from sub-millisecond to many seconds, so timeout outcomes remain uncertain.

optionExplanations.a: Remote execution depends on networks and another machine, either of which can delay, drop, or refuse work beyond the caller's control. Robust clients therefore need timeouts, retries, and failure handling absent from ordinary local calls.
optionExplanations.b: After a timeout, the caller cannot know whether the request was lost or executed and only the response was lost. This uncertain outcome is distinct from receiving a return value or a local exception.
optionExplanations.c: Retrying an operation whose response disappeared may execute it twice. Idempotence, such as deduplication keys built into the protocol, is required when duplicate effects would be harmful.
optionExplanations.d: Network latency is wildly variable: under a millisecond at good times, many seconds when the network is congested or the service overloaded. Assuming fixed latency is exactly the local-call illusion RPC encourages.

questions.question: Given the differences between local function calls and network requests, what conclusion follows for designing remote procedure call (RPC) APIs?

options.text: There is no point making a remote service look too much like a local object, since it is fundamentally different
RPC should be abandoned entirely, because REST has removed every one of these differences
Better tooling should make local and remote calls indistinguishable, so callers need not care
The differences are negligible inside one datacenter and can safely be ignored there

questions.explanation: Loss, timeouts with unknown outcome, duplicate execution on retry, variable latency, parameter encoding, and cross-language type translation all mean a remote call is fundamentally different from a local one. Hiding that (location transparency) just pushes those failures onto unprepared callers. Part of REST's appeal is that it doesn't try to hide that it is a network protocol; RPC frameworks remain useful when they acknowledge remoteness too.

questions.question: Which features show how newer RPC frameworks are more explicit that a remote request differs from a local function call? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Finagle and Rest.li use futures (promises) to represent asynchronous actions that may fail
gRPC supports streams, where one call is a series of requests and responses over time
Futures make it simpler to send requests to several services in parallel and combine results
They guarantee exactly-once execution, so retrying a call can never duplicate an action

questions.explanation: Newer RPC frameworks, built on encodings such as Thrift, Avro, Protocol Buffers (gRPC), and JSON over HTTP (Rest.li), are more explicit that remote calls are different. Futures encapsulate an asynchronous result that may fail and make parallel calls easy to combine; gRPC streams model an ongoing exchange rather than one request and one response. No framework can guarantee exactly-once execution over an unreliable network by itself: retries can still duplicate work unless the operation is idempotent.

optionExplanations.a: A future represents a result that will arrive later or may fail, so the caller must handle the asynchronous, fallible nature of the call explicitly rather than pretending it blocks like a local method.
optionExplanations.b: gRPC streams let a call consist of many requests and responses over time, acknowledging communication as an ongoing network interaction rather than a single local-style call.
optionExplanations.c: Because futures represent pending results, a caller can issue requests to multiple services concurrently and combine their results when they arrive, which is awkward with blocking local-style calls.
optionExplanations.d: Exactly-once execution cannot be guaranteed merely by an RPC framework when requests or responses can be lost. Retries may duplicate execution unless the protocol includes deduplication.

questions.question: What does a custom binary RPC protocol typically offer over JSON over REST, and what does a RESTful API offer in return?

options.text: Binary RPC can be faster; REST wins on debugging and ecosystem
REST wins on performance; RPC wins on tooling
The two are equivalent in both performance and available tooling
RPC is predominant for public APIs; REST for internal services

questions.explanation: A compact proprietary binary RPC protocol can reduce CPU and bandwidth inside a controlled organization. REST commonly wins at public boundaries because standard HTTP tools, broad client support, readable payloads, and easy debugging matter more than the last increment of wire efficiency.

questions.question: In RPC, it is reasonable to assume that all servers are upgraded before all clients. Given that order, which compatibility is needed for requests and for responses?

options.text: Backward compatibility on requests, forward compatibility on responses
Forward compatibility on requests, backward compatibility on responses
Backward compatibility on both requests and responses
No compatibility, since servers finish upgrading before clients change

questions.explanation: With servers upgraded first, a new server must handle requests from old clients: new code reading old data, which is backward compatibility on requests. Old clients must handle responses from new servers: old code reading new data, which is forward compatibility on responses. Compatibility is still needed even though servers go first, because old clients keep running throughout, and often indefinitely.

questions.question: Which statements accurately describe where RPC and web-service APIs get their compatibility properties? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Thrift, gRPC, and Avro RPC evolve according to the compatibility rules of their encoding formats
SOAP requests and responses use XML schemas, which can evolve but have some subtle pitfalls
For JSON REST APIs, adding optional request parameters or new response fields is usually compatible
All RPC schemes have the same compatibility, because compatibility comes from the transport

questions.explanation: An RPC scheme inherits its backward and forward compatibility from whatever encoding it uses. Thrift, gRPC (Protocol Buffers), and Avro RPC follow their binary schema rules; SOAP follows XML Schema with its own pitfalls; typical JSON REST APIs rely on conventions such as treating new optional request parameters and new response fields as compatible changes. The transport does not create compatibility by itself.

optionExplanations.a: Thrift, Protocol Buffers used by gRPC, and Avro RPC inherit the add/remove/type rules of their respective schemas. The transport does not override those byte-format semantics.
optionExplanations.b: SOAP messages follow XML schemas, which can evolve but contain subtle compatibility traps around optionality, ordering, and generated bindings. A standardized envelope does not eliminate schema design.
optionExplanations.c: Typical JSON REST APIs rely on conventions rather than one formal response schema: adding optional request parameters or response fields is usually tolerated. Clients must still ignore what they do not understand.
optionExplanations.d: Compatibility is determined by how requests and responses are encoded and interpreted, not by the fact that all travel over a transport. Different schema systems therefore expose different safe changes.

questions.question: What makes service compatibility harder than database compatibility?

options.text: Clients are often outside your control, so compatibility must last indefinitely
Services carry far more data per request than a database does, so old formats linger
Service protocols change faster than storage formats, so breaks happen more often
Services cannot use schema registries, so there is nowhere to record a version

questions.explanation: Database readers are usually deployed by the same organization that owns the data, so obsolete code can eventually be retired. Service clients may belong to customers or partners and remain unupdated indefinitely, forcing the provider to preserve old request and response contracts much longer.

questions.question: How do RESTful APIs typically let a client indicate which API version it wants?

options.text: There is no agreement; version numbers appear in URLs or Accept headers
Versioning is standardized: the version always goes in the URL
Versioning is handled automatically by HTTP content negotiation
API versioning is unnecessary if the encoding is compatible

questions.explanation: There is no universal API-versioning convention. Some services place a version in the URL, others negotiate it through `Accept` headers, and some use administrative mechanisms to select a version. Compatible evolution can reduce version proliferation but does not eliminate the need for policy.

questions.question: How does brokered asynchronous messaging combine properties of RPC and databases?

options.text: A broker stores messages temporarily while still aiming for low-latency delivery
A proxy forwards synchronous calls without retaining any message data
A database keeps messages permanently for arbitrary ad hoc querying
Peers exchange messages directly with no intermediary or buffering

questions.explanation: Like RPC, messages are normally delivered soon; like a database, an intermediary stores bytes until another process reads them. The broker or message queue buffers load and decouples sender availability from recipient availability.

questions.question: Which advantages does a message broker have over direct RPC? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It can buffer messages when the recipient is unavailable or overloaded, improving reliability
It can redeliver messages to a process that crashed, preventing them from being lost
The sender needn't know the recipient's IP address and port, and one message can reach several recipients
It guarantees consumers receive messages in exactly the order the sender produced them

questions.explanation: A broker can buffer while recipients are unavailable, redeliver after consumer failure, hide changing network locations, fan one message out to several consumers, and decouple producers from consumer identity. Ordering guarantees vary by broker and configuration, so they are not automatic.

optionExplanations.a: A broker persists or buffers messages while a recipient is down or overloaded, letting producers continue temporarily. This decouples availability and smooths bursts.
optionExplanations.b: If a consumer crashes before acknowledging work, a broker can offer the message again to another or restarted consumer. Redelivery reduces loss but may create duplicates that consumers must handle.
optionExplanations.c: Producers address a stable queue or topic rather than a changing host, and publish-subscribe can fan one message to several recipients. This decouples identity and network location.
optionExplanations.d: Ordering depends on partitions, concurrency, retries, and broker configuration; it is not universally exact. Direct RPC also has ordering nuances, so an unconditional broker guarantee is false.

questions.question: How does message-passing communication differ from RPC in direction, and what does 'asynchronous' mean here?

options.text: Usually one-way, send-and-forget; any reply goes on a separate channel
It is bidirectional and synchronous, so the sender blocks until a reply arrives
It is one-way but synchronous, blocking the sender until delivery is confirmed
It is identical to RPC in both direction and timing, differing only in encoding

questions.explanation: A producer normally publishes and continues without waiting for the consumer to process the message or return a value. If a reply is needed, it arrives later through another queue or topic, making the interaction one-way at each step rather than a blocking request/response call.

questions.question: Which statements about how message brokers are used are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A producer sends a message to a named queue or topic, and the broker delivers it to one or more consumers
A topic is one-way, but a consumer can publish to a reply queue read by the original sender
A consumer that republishes messages to another topic may need to preserve fields it doesn't recognize
Brokers impose a particular data model, so every message must be encoded as JSON

questions.explanation: One process sends a message to a named queue or topic, and the broker ensures it is delivered to one or more consumers or subscribers; there can be many producers and consumers on one topic. A topic is one-way, but consumers can publish onward or to a reply queue for request/response. Brokers treat a message as bytes plus metadata, so any encoding works; a backward- and forward-compatible encoding lets publishers and consumers change independently, and republishing consumers must take care not to drop unknown fields.

optionExplanations.a: Producers address a named queue or topic rather than a specific recipient, and the broker routes each message to one or more consumers or subscribers. Many producers and many consumers can share one topic.
optionExplanations.b: Each topic carries data one way, but a consumer can send a result to another topic or to a reply queue consumed by the original sender, building request/response on top of one-way messaging.
optionExplanations.c: If an older consumer decodes a message into objects without a slot for a new field and republishes it, the field is lost, just as with old code rewriting a database record. Unknown fields should be passed through.
optionExplanations.d: Brokers carry bytes plus metadata and do not impose JSON or any single data model. Producers and consumers can choose Avro, Protocol Buffers, JSON, or another encoding.

questions.question: What is the actor model of concurrency?

options.text: A model where logic lives in actors with private state, exchanging async messages
A model in which all state is shared between threads and protected by explicit locks
A model for distributed transactions across nodes with guaranteed message delivery
A model where each thread owns one message queue with guaranteed global ordering

questions.explanation: In the actor model, logic is encapsulated in actors instead of being run on threads that share state. Each actor typically represents one client or entity, may have local state not shared with any other actor, and communicates only by sending and receiving asynchronous messages. Each actor processes one message at a time, so it needs no locks. Message delivery is not guaranteed: in some error scenarios messages are lost, even within one process, which makes distributing actors across nodes a smaller conceptual leap.

questions.question: Why does location transparency work better in the actor model than in RPC?

options.text: Because the model already assumes messages may be lost, even locally
Because actor frameworks guarantee delivery over the network
Because actors run only on a single node
Because actor messages are delivered synchronously, like function calls

questions.explanation: Actors already communicate through asynchronous messages that may be delayed or lost even within one process. Moving the recipient to another node therefore changes latency and encoding, but not the fundamental programming model as radically as turning a reliable-looking local function call into RPC.

questions.question: How can Orleans, a distributed actor framework, support a new application version when its default message encoding does not support rolling upgrades?

options.text: Shift traffic to a parallel cluster or install a compatible serializer plug-in
Restart every actor simultaneously and discard all queued messages
Rely on the default format to become compatible without configuration
Convert all actor messages to untyped JSON at the network boundary

questions.explanation: Orleans can use a custom serializer or move clients gradually to a new cluster. Akka likewise can replace Java serialization with a schema-evolvable format. Erlang supports rolling code upgrades, but record-shape changes still require planning; framework support does not eliminate encoding compatibility work.

questions.question: Which benefits do rolling upgrades of a service bring? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: New versions can be released without service downtime
Cheaper releases encourage frequent small releases over rare big ones
Faulty releases can be detected and rolled back before affecting many users
They remove the need for compatibility, since all nodes run one version

questions.explanation: A rolling upgrade deploys a new version to a few nodes at a time rather than all at once. Because the remaining nodes keep serving, releases need no downtime, which encourages frequent small releases, and a faulty release can be caught and rolled back while it affects only a few nodes. The price is that old and new code coexist, so new code must read old data and old code must read new data.

optionExplanations.a: Old nodes keep serving traffic while new ones start, so a release does not require a service-wide outage.
optionExplanations.b: Without downtime, each release is less costly and less disruptive, which makes frequent small releases practical instead of rare large ones that bundle many changes.
optionExplanations.c: A faulty build reaches only the first few nodes, so it can be detected and rolled back before most users encounter it, which reduces the blast radius of a bad release.
optionExplanations.d: A rolling deployment deliberately creates a period when old and new versions run together. That coexistence increases the need for backward and forward compatibility rather than removing it.

questions.question: Which encoding family combines compact data with explicit schema-evolution rules?

options.text: Schema-driven binary formats such as Avro or Protocol Buffers
Language-specific native object serialization formats
Schemaless text formats such as JSON, XML, or CSV
Ad hoc positional binary records with no schema

questions.explanation: Language-specific encodings are convenient but couple data to one runtime and are often unsafe for long-lived exchange. Text formats are broadly interoperable but vague about types and compatibility. Schema-driven binary formats add compactness and defined evolution rules, at the cost of managing schemas.

questions.question: What are the three common modes of dataflow between processes in which encoding compatibility matters?

options.text: Through databases, service calls (REST and RPC), and asynchronous message passing
Through CPU caches, through main memory, and through local disk, each with its own data layout
Through batch processing, through stream processing, and through interactive queries
Through shared memory, through operating-system pipes, and through process signals

questions.explanation: Encoding is needed whenever data goes to a process that doesn't share memory. In a database, the writer encodes and a later reader decodes. In REST and RPC, the client encodes a request, the server decodes it and encodes a response, and the client decodes the response. In asynchronous message passing, through brokers or actors, the sender encodes and the recipient decodes. In each mode compatibility is a relationship between the encoding process and the decoding process, which may run different code versions.
